In [[potential theory]] and optimization, '''polarization constants''' (also known as '''Chebyshev constants''') are solutions to a max-min problem for potentials. Originally,  these problems were introduced by a Japanese mathematician [[Makoto Ohtsuka]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Ohtsuka | first1=Makoto
| title=On various definitions of capacity and related notions
| journal=Nagoya Mathematical Journal
| volume=30
| year=1967
| pages=121–127
| doi=10.1017/S0027763000012411 | doi-access=free}}</ref> Recently these problems got some attention as they can help to generate [[random]] points on smooth [[manifolds]] (in particular, [[unit sphere]]) with prescribed [[probability density function]]. The problem of finding the polarization constant is connected to the problem of [[energy minimization]] and, in particular to the [[Thomson problem]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Farkas | first1=Bálint
| last2=Révész | first2=Szilárd Gy.
| title=Potential theoretic approach to rendezvous numbers
| journal=Monatshefte für Mathematik
| volume=148
| year=2006
| issue=4
| pages=309–331
| doi=10.1007/s00605-006-0397-5 | doi-access=free| arxiv=math/0503423
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Borodachov | first1=Sergiy V.
| last2=Hardin | first2=Douglas P.
| last3=Reznikov | first3=Alexander
| last4=Saff | first4=Edward B.
| title=Optimal discrete measures for Riesz potentials
| journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
| volume=370
| issue=10
| year=2018
| pages=6973–6993
| doi=10.1090/tran/7224| arxiv=1606.04128
| s2cid=119285365
}}</ref>

==Practical motivation==
From the practical point of view, these problems can be used to answer the following question: if <math>K(x,x_j)</math> denotes the amount of a substance received at <math>x</math> due to an injector of the substance located
at <math>x_j</math>, what is the smallest number of like injectors and their optimal locations on <math>A</math> so that a prescribed minimal amount of the substance
reaches every point of <math>A</math>? For example, one can relate this question to treating [[tumors]] with [[radioactive]] seeds. 

==Formal Definition==
More precisely, for a compact set <math>A</math> and  kernel <math>K:A\times A \to \mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}</math>, the discrete polarization  problem is the following:  determine <math>N</math>-point configurations <math>\{x_j\}_{j=1}^N</math> on <math>A</math> so that the minimum of <math>\sum_{j=1}^N K(x,x_j)</math> for <math>x\in A</math> is as large as possible.

==Classical kernels==
The Chebyshev nomenclature for this max-min problem emanates from the case when <math>K</math> is the logarithmic kernel,  <math>K(x,y)=\log |x-y|^{-1},</math>  for when <math>A</math> is a subset of
the complex plane, the problem is equivalent to finding the constrained <math>N</math>-th degree [[Chebyshev polynomial]] for <math>A</math>; that is, the [[monic polynomial]] in the complex variable <math>z</math> with all its zeros on <math>A</math> having
minimal uniform norm on <math>A</math>.

If <math>A</math> is the [[unit circle]] in the plane and <math>K(x,y)=|x-y|^{-s}</math>, <math>s>0</math> (i.e., kernel of a [[Riesz potential]]), then <math>N</math> equally spaced points on the circle solve the <math>N</math> point polarization problem.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Ambrus | first1=Gergely
| last2=Ball | first2=Keith M. | authorlink2=Keith Ball
| last3=Erdélyi | first3=Tamás
| title=Chebyshev constants for the unit circle
| journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society
| volume=45
| year=2013
| issue=2
| pages=236–248
| doi=10.1112/blms/bds082| arxiv=1006.5153
| s2cid=2989181
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Hardin | first1=Douglas P.
